title: How the barcode was invented: Woodland and Silver, George Laurer's UPC, and the first scan in 1974

sources.title: IBM Engineer Who Designed The Universal Bar Code Dies At 94 (2019-12-12)
Beep! The barcode turns 50, who invented it? (2023-04-04)

facts.text: In 1948 the head of a local grocery chain came to Drexel University in Philadelphia seeking a way to read product information automatically at the checkout.
Bernard Silver and Norman Joseph Woodland, two Drexel graduate students, developed an early barcode system.
Woodland said the pattern was inspired by the Morse code he had learned in the Boy Scouts; he extended the dots and dashes downward into narrow and wide lines.
The patent application was filed on October 20, 1949, and the patent was granted in 1952.
Their code was a bull's-eye of concentric circles that could be scanned from any direction.
Reliable scanning machines did not yet exist when the barcode was invented, and laser scanning took a long time to catch up.
Grocers at first opposed a universal system, and food canners disliked the idea and cost of printing codes on their products.
IBM engineer George Laurer was asked to write a proposal for making the bull's-eye code work in supermarkets, but instead designed a linear barcode.
Laurer judged the circular code unworkable because it was too small and would smear on the poor-quality printing presses used for most food labels.
In 1973 the grocery industry chose the barcode proposed by Laurer and IBM as its standard; Woodland joined the team to help refine it.
In June 1974 a cashier at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, rang up a pack of Juicy Fruit chewing gum using the new Universal Product Code; it was the first product scanned this way.
Between 1976 and 1980 the number of stores using IBM's barcode rose from 104 to 2,207.
IBM did not patent the UPC and largely gave it away in order to sell scanning equipment.
Laurer expected the barcode to be replaced by another technology within about a decade.
Barcodes are now scanned more than 6 billion times a day, according to GS1.
Derived: 2,207 is about 21 times 104; the 1974 scan came about 25 years after the 1949 patent filing.
